entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The European Free Trade Association (EFTA), founded in 1960 in Geneva, Switzerland, was a pioneering international trade organization and free trade area that aimed to promote economic cooperation among its member states.

Established by the European Economic Community (EEC), a precursor to the European Union, EFTA brought together five European countries—Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, and Sweden—to negotiate trade agreements and establish a common external tariff.

The EFTA's significance lies in its role as a precursor to the European Union's single market, as it paved the way for the creation of the European Economic Area (EEA) in 1994, which integrated Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein into the EU's internal market.

EFTA's legacy extends beyond the realm of trade, as it also played a crucial role in shaping the European Union's economic policies and influencing the development of the single market.

As the EFTA celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2010, its impact on the European economy and the world of international trade remained a testament to its enduring influence.
